claims.claim: High-cost cities pay an order of magnitude more per subway mile than the global norm: the Transit Costs Project's database of 900+ projects averages almost $350 million per mile, while Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 is projected near $4 billion per mile.
claims.episode_span: In high-cost cities a single mile of new subway routinely lands between one and three billion dollars, while comparable tunnels elsewhere finish for two or three hundred million.
claims.source_title: Why it costs $4 billion per mile of subway track | Vital City
claims.supporting_quote: the average project costs almost $350 million per mile. Phase 2 of the Second Avenue Subway is projected to cost close to $4 billion per mile, or more than 11 times the global average.

claims.claim: The cost differential between cities is explained by process factors — politics, procurement, utilities and agency coordination, labor, and design choices — rather than by the physical work itself.
claims.episode_span: The difference is not geology or tunnel diameter. It sits in the layers of process, contract structure, and accumulated delay that sit on top of the physical work.
claims.source_title: Why it costs $4 billion per mile of subway track | Vital City
claims.supporting_quote: we show how politics and decision-making, civil service and internal capacity, procurement and risk allocation, utilities and agency coordination, labor, and cost-effective design explain this massive cost differential.

claims.claim: Stations, not the bored tunnel, account for most of an urban line's cost: Second Avenue Subway Phase 1 station contracts were 77% of its $3.16 billion construction cost.
claims.episode_span: the billion-dollar headline figures bundle stations, systems, and fit-out — which routinely account for most of an urban line's cost
claims.source_title: Why it costs $4 billion per mile of subway track | Vital City
claims.supporting_quote: This is important because station construction is expensive. Phase 1’s station contracts accounted for 77% of the project’s $3.16 billion in total construction costs.

claims.claim: U.S. transit projects lack standardization and tend to make stations bespoke, unlike lower-cost countries that standardize designs.
claims.episode_span: each new station is treated as a signature civic building with custom architecture, artwork requirements, and bespoke mechanical systems
claims.source_title: Why transit projects cost more in the U.S. than almost anywhere else | High Speed Rail Alliance
claims.supporting_quote: The relative lack of standardization in U.S. projects is a third key factor. Countries with lower construction costs emphasize standardization

claims.claim: Utility owners and government agencies frequently hold up transit projects with their own demands, making relocations a source of delay and cost.
claims.episode_span: Utility companies own the rights to move their own pipes and cables, so every relocation becomes a separate negotiation that can stretch for months while crews wait.
claims.source_title: Why transit projects cost more in the U.S. than almost anywhere else | High Speed Rail Alliance
claims.supporting_quote: how often government agencies or utility companies gum up these projects because they want something

claims.claim: Primarily tunneled rail projects cost under $300 million per mile in South Korea, Chile, Norway and Italy and over $500 million in Germany and Japan, while the U.S. averages $582 million per mile - over $1.3 billion per mile once two short New York City tunnels are included.
claims.episode_span: In high-cost cities a single mile of new subway routinely lands between one and three billion dollars, while comparable tunnels elsewhere finish for two or three hundred million.
claims.source_title: On the Right Track: Rail Transit Project Delivery Around the World - Eno Center for Transportation
claims.supporting_quote: Construction costs for primarily tunneled projects range from under $300 million per mile in South Korea, Chile, Norway, and Italy to over $500 million in Germany and Japan. The United States averages over $1.3 billion per mile if including two short, tunneled projects in New York City, or $582 million per mile on average if they are excluded.

claims.claim: The U.S. pays 57 percent more per mile for below-ground lines than the rest of Eno's database, and the U.S. tunneling premium rises to 263 percent when New York City's recent tunneled projects are included.
claims.episode_span: the documented cost spread between otherwise similar projects still exceeds what those upgrades alone would explain, pointing again to the surrounding process layers.
claims.source_title: On the Right Track: Rail Transit Project Delivery Around the World - Eno Center for Transportation
claims.supporting_quote: the United States pays 48 percent more on a per-mile basis to build primarily at-grade transit projects, and 57 percent more for below-ground lines. This cost premium holds for both tunneled and at-grade projects. When including the disproportionately expensive tunneled projects recently completed in New York City, the U.S. tunneling premium rises to 263 percent.

claims.claim: NYU's Transit Costs Project finds New York transit projects cost 20 times more per kilometer than Seoul's, drawing on a database of more than 11,000 km of urban rail across 50+ countries built since the late 1990s.
claims.episode_span: A mile of subway can cost two billion dollars in one city and a tenth that in another
claims.source_title: Transit Costs Project | Marron Institute of Urban Management, NYU
claims.supporting_quote: Why do transit-infrastructure projects in New York cost 20 times more on a per kilometer basis than in Seoul? We investigate this question across hundreds of transit projects from around the world. We have created a database that spans more than 50 countries and totals more than 11,000 km of urban rail built since the late 1990s.

claims.claim: U.S. urban rail projects carry a premium of more than 50 percent over international peers for both at-grade and tunneled lines, despite being simpler in engineering terms.
claims.episode_span: The difference is not geology or tunnel diameter.
claims.source_title: Comparing the Costs of Transit Projects: New Report and Interactive Graphs - Eno Center for Transportation
claims.supporting_quote: The US pays more than a 50 percent premium to build at-grade and tunneled rail projects despite its projects being relatively simpler in terms of engineering aspects.
